criteria.note: A bolded 'short answer' naming the specific wheat-free potato, corn and rice snacks lands around word 140, well inside the first 200 words.

Rendered title is 59 characters including the appended suffix, the description is ~140 characters, and the two share no phrasing; keyword tokens are present, though only via the 'GF' abbreviation plus the site suffix.
Headings carry the argument on their own — bad news first, what passes, the flavor trap, the non-snack traps, staples, then the celiac honesty section — so a skim reproduces the piece's logic.
Four distinct internal destinations, each earned at the moment the reader needs it (the label guide at the four-word scan, the hidden-gluten guide at 양조간장, the pillar guide as an entry point).
All three FAQ answers are established in the body — the survivor list, the Orion flavor split, and the three celiac caveats — and each reads as a standalone answer.

First-hand signal is specific and dated: a stint working in a convenience store, the household's flip-and-scan routine, an April 2026 pull of CU's 211-item catalog with a real bucket breakdown, and an admitted miss (반숙계란장) that went the wrong way.

Product names carry Korean plus romanisation (포카칩 오리지널 / Pocachip Original, 참쌀설병 / Chamssal Seolbyeong), the allergen declarations are quoted as 우유·대두·쇠고기 vs 밀, and the catalog counts (81/39/75/16 of 211) are checkable.

Orion's manufacturer product page and the 법제처 시행규칙 별표 2 text are both linked with explicit retrieval dates, and the secondary blog roundup is labelled with its publication date and its age flagged as a weakness.

The method's limits are stated bluntly ('It can flag what's obviously wheat; it cannot clear anything'), the celiac-vs-NCGS standard is disclosed, secondary sourcing is labelled as such, and there are no commercial links.

findings.quote: Korean Convenience Store GF Snack Guide
findings.why: The target keyword is spelled out as "gluten free" by searchers, but the title proper abbreviates it to "GF" and the description never uses the phrase at all — exact-match presence depends entirely on the appended ' | Gluten-Free Korea' suffix. That is a thin margin for the primary query.
findings.fix: Rewrite as e.g. 'Gluten-Free Korean Convenience Store Snacks' (44 chars + 20-char suffix = 64 — or drop 'Convenience Store' to 'Gluten-Free Korean Snacks: Convenience Store Guide' variants under 40) so the keyword appears in the title proper, and work 'gluten-free' into the description opener.

findings.quote: Some are made without wheat. But 'no wheat flour' is not the same as celiac-safe, and Korea's allergen line only flags wheat — so read the full ingredient list (원재료명) on the specific package.
findings.why: Every FAQ answer is body-supported, but answers 1 and 3 run well past the ~300-character window Google renders in an FAQ rich result, so the useful part (the survivor list, the celiac caveats) risks being truncated away.
findings.fix: Front-load each answer with a one-sentence verdict under 300 characters, then keep the detail in the body rather than the markup.

findings.why: Every other heading carries the argument on its own ('the fridge is a lost cause', 'The flavor trap'); this one is a generic label and wastes the last skim-stop before the link list.
findings.fix: Retitle to something that states the takeaway, e.g. 'Shop the snack aisle, never the fridge — and never trust a brand'.

criteria.note: Nearly every factual claim is either linked to a source (Orion product page, the 2023 Korean roundup, the 시행규칙 별표 2 text) or explicitly framed as the author's own catalog pass, but a small number of permissive claims in the drinks/ice-cream section rest on nothing but assertion.
criteria.evidence_quote: Standard green-bottle 소주 is a distilled spirit; flavored sojus and everything else in that door are blended products, so the 원재료명 applies there like everywhere else.

criteria.note: Product names are real and specific, the CU counts are internally consistent (81+39+75+16 = 211), and the retrieval/publication dates line up with the stated update history.

The piece names its method as a keyword pass over product names and categories, states outright that it cannot clear anything, and even reports a concrete miss (반숙계란장) plus the single-chain, single-season scope; the snack list is likewise disclosed as second-hand rather than tested.

No absolute safety claims, cross-contamination and shared lines are addressed explicitly, and the author separates his household's non-celiac standard from the stricter celiac bar rather than conflating them.
Every source carries a date, the two-year age of the roundup is flagged as a problem in a silently reformulating market, and the statute is marked as amendable with a re-check instruction.
The load-bearing labelling fact is correct and correctly attributed to 식품등의 표시·광고에 관한 법률 시행규칙 별표 2 (제5조제1항), and the Korean terms, product categories and 양조간장/엿기름/보리차 explanations are accurate.
Readers get a manufacturer allergen page, a direct law.go.kr link, the four-character scan (밀 / 소맥 / 보리 / 호밀), and an instruction to read the full 원재료명 rather than the allergen line.

findings.quote: Standard green-bottle 소주 is a distilled spirit; flavored sojus and everything else in that door are blended products, so the 원재료명 applies there like everywhere else.
findings.why: This is the one permissive claim on the page with no source and no 'I haven't verified this' marker — a reader could treat 'distilled spirit' as a clearance for the plain green bottle. The neighbouring ice-cream line ('the ice cream is often fine') has the same shape. Neither is likely to cause gluten ingestion, but both break the sourcing discipline the rest of the article holds to.
findings.fix: Either cite a manufacturer or 원재료명 for a named soju/ice bar, or mark these as the author's working assumption in the same way the CU pass and the snack list are marked.

findings.quote: Gluten-free Korean snacks that pass: potato, corn, rice
findings.why: The heading asserts 'gluten-free' and 'pass' for a list that the very next paragraph correctly downgrades to unverified, second-hand, wheat-absence-only leads. The correction is immediate and unmistakable, so this does not reach a lapse, but headings are what gets skimmed, quoted and screenshotted — and this one says more than the evidence does.
findings.fix: Retitle to match the body's own standard, e.g. 'Snacks worth flipping over: potato, corn, rice' or 'Reported wheat-free snacks: potato, corn, rice'.
